description:
## Why this ticket exists

**ISS-046** established that tracked files carry the maintainer's real email, account name and home path, which the project's hard rule forbids in anything checked in. An issue records a finding; it cannot be a dependency. **T-009's privacy preflight is a repository-wide scan, so T-009 cannot pass its own first gate until this is done** — `T-009.blockedBy` contains this ticket.

Occurrences are named by file, line and PATTERN CLASS, never quoted. Quoting the value is the defect ISS-046 itself committed and corrected.

**Scope grew after plan review round 4.** The reviewer's finding: T-024 inventoried the account/email/path classes, but T-009's scan also covers **session identifiers**, and the repository has those too — so completing the narrow ticket would not have made the broad scan passable, which is the only thing this ticket exists to do. The classifier was therefore run for real over all 279 tracked files before rewriting this ticket, and the inventory below is its output, not a guess.

**The scanner itself moved here from T-009 §8.** A blocker whose completion is defined by a check that lives in the ticket it unblocks cannot be verified independently. T-024 builds and runs the scanner; T-009 consumes it as a preflight.

## Scan domain — two modes, deliberately not one

The scan never reads the dirty working tree; transient tool-written fields live there between operations and must simply never reach a commit. But plan review round 5 found that "HEAD plus the index" is not one domain and cannot be one decision:

- **Pre-commit mode reads the PROSPECTIVE COMMITTED TREE — the index alone**: staged blobs for modified paths, index entries for everything unchanged. Scanning HEAD as well would make remediation impossible, because during the very commit that removes a leak, HEAD still contains it and the staged replacement is clean, so a combined scan fails and refuses to authorize the fix. Combining the two also double-counts modified paths and makes line-anchored findings ambiguous about which version they refer to.
- **Audit mode reads HEAD**, for post-commit verification and for reporting on the repository as it stands. It is not part of the pre-commit decision.

## Enforcement boundary — stated honestly, because it is not absolute

Round 5: proving a guard command *can* reject a staged file says nothing about every commit going through it. A repository script or an opt-in local hook does not stop Storybloq's own writes, another worktree, or `git commit --no-verify`.

- **Preferred fix, unavailable here:** stop the external serializer writing personal claim values. The writer is the `@storybloq/storybloq` MCP server, outside this repository, so this ticket cannot do it. Recorded as the fix that would actually close the class, not silently skipped.
- **What this ticket does instead, and it must actually be installed:** a commit wrapper that autonomous workflows are required to use, invoking pre-commit mode; and a **real CI workflow running audit mode on every pushed commit**. Round 6 caught that an earlier revision claimed CI enforcement while the repository has **no `.github/workflows` at all** — reproduced 2026-08-01 — so the claim described nothing. The repo does have a GitHub remote, so the workflow will run once pushed. Both integrations carry a mutation proving they fail closed; a criterion that only requires the scanner to work would let this ticket complete with its stated enforcement absent.
- **Documented plainly:** local bypass remains possible — `--no-verify`, another worktree, or a tool writing outside the wrapper. Without a server-side protected-branch check this is **detection, not prevention**, and the ticket does not claim the class is closed.

## Inventory (classifier output, 2026-08-01, 279 tracked files)

The classifier found **18 distinct UUIDs** and **14 distinct account names** in path positions. Most are the repo's documented synthetic conventions and are correctly permitted — `testuser` (27 occurrences), `fixture*`, `realperson`, `u`, `x`, `me`, and the zero-padded `019c0000-0000-7000-8000-0000000000NN` id family. The real values are these:

### Class A — real account name / email / home path in tracked files

- **A1.** `.story/tickets/T-009.json`, fields `.claim.user` (email) and `.claim.claimedBySession` (real session id). **Not fixable by editing, and the writer is outside this repo. Reproduced:** the value equals `git config user.email`; the writer is the Storybloq MCP server's ticket-claim serializer, not code in this repository. It IS removed when the claim is released — T-008 is `complete` and carries no `claim` object, and exactly one file in the whole tracker has the field: the one currently claimed. **But transient is not safe:** `git log -S` over all refs finds the email in commits `8f9d799` and `304da06`, so a ticket claimed at commit time puts it in history. That is the observed default, not a hypothetical. **Remediation is a commit-time guard, not a scrub.**
- **A2.** `product-architecture-2026-07-30.md:10` — a real home path in path-mangled form plus a real session id, in one blockquote. Line 5 of the same file carries a second real session id. The only class-A occurrences outside `.story/` and the test suite.
- **A3.** `.story/issues/ISS-005.json` — 2 occurrences of the home-path class. Report text quoting the strings the issue was filed to remove from `src/`.
- **A4.** `.story/tickets/T-007.json` — 1 occurrence of that same report class.

### Class B — deliberate denylist specifications (REMOVE them; round 5 killed the exemption idea)

These name a real value as a string a scan must SEARCH FOR. Revisions of this ticket proposed keeping them behind an exact machine-readable exemption set. **Round 5 rejected that, and it is right:** the hard rule permits no real personal value in anything checked in. An exemption list makes the violation explicit; it does not make it permissible, and "the exemption set is exactly these entries" is a well-audited way of still having the values in the repository.

So every real class-B literal is **removed**, and the guard keeps its power by **committed semantic rules alone**. Round 6 killed the salted-digest idea that briefly replaced it: a digest whose input lives in untracked local configuration cannot enforce anything on a fresh clone or in CI, so the check would pass only on one machine and silently degrade everywhere else — which is worse than the literal it replaced, because it *looks* enforced.

The realisation that makes this work: the tarball audits in T-007 and T-023 never needed the specific historical values. `grep for <account> | <rollout-id>` is a weaker, hand-maintained version of "run the classifier over the unpacked tarball". So those steps are replaced by a call to the scanner in directory mode, which knows the classes and needs no secrets, no local config and no literals. **The committed exemption set is required to be empty**, and no CI secret is introduced, because none is needed.

- **B1.** `.story/tickets/T-007.json` — 2 account-name occurrences and 3 session-id occurrences inside tarball-audit grep patterns.
- **B2.** `.story/tickets/T-023.json` — 1 account-name occurrence, same audit step.
- **B3.** `tests-ts/contract/packaging.contract.mjs:249` — 1 account-name occurrence in a comment explaining the historical leak the test prevents.
- **B4.** `.story/issues/ISS-005.json`, `.story/issues/ISS-037.json` — 1 session-id occurrence each, referencing the same denylisted id.

### Class C — real session identifiers outside the claim block (found by the round-4 rerun)

This class is why the ticket was rewritten. None of it was in the original inventory.

- **C1.** `.story/handovers/2026-07-31-02-checkpoint.md:3` — a real Claude Code session id in a `**Session:**` header.
- **C2.** `.story/issues/ISS-018.json`, `.story/issues/ISS-019.json` — the same id, in impact text.
- **C3.** `.story/handovers/2026-07-31-01-spendbar-plan-approved-name-claimed.md:12` and `product-architecture-2026-07-30.md:5` — a real Codex rollout id.

**Reproduced: there is no generator to chase.** Only 4 of 11 handovers carry a `**Session:**` header at all, so the field is written by the authoring agent, not emitted by a template. That makes it a **habit class**, not a generated-field class — no single fix removes it, and the next handover reintroduces it unless a check refuses. The remediation is therefore the same commit-time guard as A1, widened: it must reject a real-identity session id anywhere under `.story/**`, not only in claim fields.

Two further shapes the classifier's tracked-only view did not show, both found by scanning the untracked tree as well:

- Handovers also embed session ids inside `.story/sessions/<id>/plan.md` **path references** in prose, not just in headers. A check anchored on the `**Session:**` header would miss those.
- **9 of the 11 handovers are currently untracked** (class D), and handovers are meant to be committed. So most of this class is not in the repository yet and is entirely invisible to a `git ls-files` scan — which is exactly the gap the commit-time guard closes, and exactly why a scan alone is not the deliverable.

### Class D — untracked working-tree files at repo root

Not in the repository, so not a disclosure — but one `git add -A` from being one, and invisible to a gate that reads only `git ls-files`. Decide per file: scrub, delete, or `.gitignore`.

- **D1.** `git-activity-review-2026-07-01-to-2026-07-15.md` — 13 account-name occurrences.
- **D2.** `westworld-investigation-2026-07-15.md` — 1.
- **D3.** Nine untracked handovers under `.story/handovers/`, of which **6 carry a real session id** (`2026-07-31-05`, `2026-08-01-02`, `2026-08-01-03` in a `**Session:**` header; `2026-08-01-04` in both a path reference and a reviewer-session reference; `2026-08-01-05` in a path reference) and one (`2026-07-31-04`) carries an account-name occurrence. Unlike D1 and D2, these are **intended to be committed** — they are the project's own session record — so "delete or gitignore" is not an acceptable disposition for them and they must be scrubbed.

## Scope

**Out:**

- **Rewriting git history.** The values exist in past commits, including `1cc1ff9`, `8f9d799` and `304da06`. Whether to rewrite published history is an owner decision with its own consequences and is NOT proposed here. This ticket cleans HEAD and the index, and says so plainly rather than implying the values are gone.
- Wiring the scan into T-009's gate sequence — T-009 §8 does that. T-024 delivers the command and leaves it green.

## Constraints (hard rules)

- **A report about a forbidden value names the file, line and class — never the value.** Established by ISS-046 after its own first version quoted the real home path into tracked text, and reinforced when ISS-037 and ISS-038, filed the same session, were found to have the same defect. Everything this ticket writes obeys it, including the closing notes.
- Replacements use documented synthetic placeholders of the same shape (`testuser`, the `019c0000-…` id family) so the surrounding text still demonstrates what it was demonstrating.
- No unrelated edits ride along in the diff.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **A2, A3, A4, C1, C2, C3 are replaced with documented synthetic placeholders.** For C1/C3, if a generator emits the field, the recorded finding names the generator and the fix is applied there as well as in the existing files — otherwise the next handover reintroduces it.
2. **A1 and the C/D session-id classes are closed by a commit-time guard**, not a scrub: a check that fails when staged `.story/**` content carries a real-identity value of any covered class — the `claim.user` and `claim.claimedBySession` fields, and session identifiers anywhere in the text, including inside `.story/sessions/<id>/…` path references. Verified by **staging an offending file of each shape and observing the guard reject it** — not by observing it pass on a clean tree, which proves nothing. A guard anchored on field names or on the `**Session:**` header alone fails criterion 6's semantic test and does not satisfy this.
3. **Every class-B literal is removed from tracked files**, replaced by committed semantic rules — never by a digest or literal sourced from untracked local configuration, which cannot enforce on a fresh clone. The tarball-audit steps in T-007 and T-023 are rewritten to call the scanner in directory mode over the unpacked tarball, and **a test proves the replacement still rejects the value the literal used to name**, running from a clean checkout with no local configuration present.
4. **Each class-D file is scrubbed, deleted, or gitignored**, with the choice recorded per file — except the untracked handovers, which are part of the project's session record and must be **scrubbed**, since deleting or ignoring them destroys the thing they exist to preserve.
5b. **Both integrations are installed, not merely possible, and each is tested on its own.**

   - **The commit wrapper** invokes pre-commit (index) mode. Tested directly: stage a leak, invoke the wrapper, and require it to **refuse the commit** — before CI is involved at all. Plan review round 7 caught that the earlier mutation ("remove the wrapper's scanner call and require CI to reject the commit") tested only the CI backstop, so a permanently broken wrapper would satisfy it whenever CI happened to work.
   - **CI scans every commit in the push, not just the tip.** A push-triggered workflow that audits the checked-out HEAD passes when a leak is introduced in one commit and removed in the next, while the forbidden value sits in remote history forever. So CI **enumerates every new commit in the event range** using the scanner's `--mode=commit --rev=<sha>`, and handles the two ranges that have no `before` commit: a newly created branch and a force push.
   - Tested with a **two-commit push fixture where only the first commit leaks**, which must fail.
   - The workflow's own invocation is mutation-tested locally, so a broken CI step fails rather than passing silently.
   - If the owner declines a CI workflow, this criterion is **not** waived quietly — the CI claim is struck from the ticket and the prevention gap is recorded as unresolved.

5. **The scanner exists as a runnable command with five modes** — `index` (pre-commit, the prospective committed tree), `worktree` (tracked paths on disk, what `git add -A` would stage), `audit` (HEAD), `commit --rev=<treeish>` (any commit, for CI push ranges), and `dir --dir=<path>` (an unpacked tarball). It covers emails, macOS/Linux/Windows home paths, path-mangled home directories, UUID session identifiers and non-UUID workflow identifiers. Repo-backed modes skip `node_modules` and `.git`; **`dir` mode excludes nothing but `.git`**, because `dist` is exactly what ships and skipping it would recreate the blind spot that let personal data into a published package while the packaging contract stayed green.
   Required properties, each with a test that fails without it: symlinks are **not followed** and their target text is scanned; UTF-16 is decoded rather than dismissed as binary; a binary file whose extension is not declared is **reported as unscannable** rather than skipped; a scan that read zero text files **refuses to report a pass**; and an unknown mode is a hard error that never falls back to `index`.
   A test proves `index` and `worktree` disagree in the case that matters — a leak edited into a tracked file but not yet staged is invisible to `index` and must be caught by `worktree`.
6. **It is semantic, and that is demonstrated, not asserted.** For **every** class, a test presents a documented synthetic value and a real-shaped counterpart of that same class and requires opposite verdicts. The allowlist matches by **exact equality (accounts) or fully anchored pattern (identifiers), never by prefix** — review found prefix matching cleared an undeclared account that merely began with a declared one, and accepted a synthetic session-id prefix followed by arbitrary real-looking data. Negative fixtures for both cases are required. A scanner that cannot make these distinctions is a string match with extra steps.
7. **The scan passes with an EMPTY exemption set**, and a test asserts the exemption set is empty rather than merely asserting no unexpected hits — the latter passes vacuously when the scan finds nothing at all, and any non-empty set is a real value still in the repository. Separately, a fixture with a known planted value must make the scan fail, so a green run is evidence the scan works and not evidence it looked nowhere.
8. **Nothing this ticket writes contains a real personal value** — verified by running criterion 5's scanner against this ticket's own diff.
9. **The out-of-scope git-history exposure is stated explicitly in the closing note**, so "scrubbed" is never read as "removed from the repository's history".

## Risks

The failure mode is the sibling-miss pattern in `docs/v0.2-prototype-findings.md` §4.1: fixing the occurrence that surfaced and not its siblings. That pattern is how this ticket exists — ISS-046 was filed, corrected, then a wider scan found the same defect in ISS-037 and ISS-038; then plan review round 4 found the whole session-identifier class missing from the inventory. Each round the fix was real and each round it was too narrow. Criterion 7 is written as a total scan with an exact exemption set for that reason, and criterion 1 requires chasing generated fields to their generator rather than to the file that happened to surface.

The second risk is that scrubbing HEAD reads as remediation while the values remain in history and in every existing clone. Criterion 9 exists to stop that misreading.


## EXECUTION RECORD (2026-08-02) — dispositions and closing note

**Delivered:** `scripts/privacy-scan.mjs` (five modes: index / worktree / audit / commit / dir; seven semantic classes plus `unscannable-binary` and `malformed-encoding` fail-closed reports), `scripts/privacy-synthetic.json` (synthetic conventions only — a test pins the key set so an exemption list cannot appear), `scripts/guarded-commit.mjs` (index-mode gate, fail-closed, fixture-repo tested end-to-end), `.github/workflows/privacy.yml` (enumerates every commit in the push range via `--mode=commit`, handles new branches and force pushes, refuses to pass vacuously), and `tests-ts/privacy-scan.test.mjs` (19 tests). The scanner was reviewed as code across four external review rounds; the findings and fixes are recorded in the T-009 plan §12, rounds 7–10.

**Class A dispositions:**
- A1 (claim fields): closed by the commit-time guard, not a scrub, as specified. The worktree copy of T-009.json legitimately carries the fields between operations; `guarded-commit` scans the index, and the T-024 commit staged T-009.json with the claim block stripped, leaving the worktree copy for the tool that owns the lease.
- A2 (architecture doc): real session ids removed from the provenance note; the machine-specific transcript path replaced with a note stating why it is not recorded and how the owner reconstructs it.
- A3/A4 (ISS-005, T-007 report text): home path → `/Users/testuser` (the shape is what the text illustrates); the quoted `USER=` value → an angle-bracket placeholder.

**Class B dispositions — all literals REMOVED, none kept:**
- `packaging.contract.mjs`: the three hand-rolled content greps (name literal, UUID-suffix rule, home-path check with a generic-name placeholder set) replaced by the semantic scanner over every shipped byte, plus a fragment-assembled test proving the scanner still catches each class the literals named, plus a maintainer-identity check whose tokens derive from `git config` at runtime — the repository carries no name literal, and the check bites wherever a human packs, which is the only place publishing happens (T-007 forbids autonomous publish).
- T-007 / T-023 audit-step text: grep literals replaced with angle-bracket placeholders and pointers to `--mode=dir` over the unpacked tarball.
- Bare-name occurrences in ISS-005/ISS-018 resolutions and handover 2026-07-31-01 (npm account name): placeholders.

**Class C dispositions:** the real session id and the real rollout id scrubbed from both tracked handovers, ISS-018, ISS-019 and the architecture doc; identifiers were REMOVED with an explicit marker rather than replaced, because substituting a synthetic id into a historical record would fabricate history. The workflow id in handover 2026-07-31-04 likewise. Confirmed there is no generator to chase: only 4 of 11 handovers carried a `**Session:**` header, so the field is authored, not templated — the commit guard is what stops recurrence.

**Class D dispositions:** the two review documents at the repo root are `.gitignore`d by exact name (not deleted — they are the owner's working notes; not globbed — future notes get their own decision). All nine untracked handovers were scrubbed in place, since they are the project's session record and must remain committable.

**Fixture renames (scanner-flagged generic accounts):** fixtures in `core.test.mjs`, `resolve.test.mjs` and `unicode-parity.test.mjs` used single-letter or generic account names in home-path positions — names a real contributor could actually have, which is why the tightened allowlist rejects them. Each was renamed to `fixture` or `testuser` (the unicode-parity corpus is computed live on both the TS and Python side, so renames cannot break parity), and the `verify.py` comment was reworded to avoid a truncated mangled run. The old names are deliberately not quoted here: while writing this very record, quoting them re-created the finding in this file, and the scanner caught it before staging — the fifth self-referential instance this session, and the first one caught by the delivered tooling instead of by review. All suites re-run green (355 + 20 contract + 19 scanner).

**Verification state at close:** `--mode=worktree` reports exactly 2 findings — T-009.json's tool-written claim fields, the designed guard case — and 0 anywhere else across 303 text files. Index mode green at commit time with the stripped-claim staging. A planted-value fixture, an examined-zero-files refusal, and per-class synthetic/real discrimination tests all prove the scan can fail.

**CLOSING NOTE, per criterion 9:** this ticket cleaned HEAD, the index and the working tree. **The scrubbed values remain in git history** — including commits `1cc1ff9`, `8f9d799` and `304da06` — and in every existing clone. "Scrubbed" here never means "removed from the repository's history"; whether to rewrite published history is an owner decision this ticket explicitly does not make.
title: Make the repository pass a personal-data scan, and build the scanner that says so (ISS-046)
